failing_part: "gives near-nominal type I error even with about 12 units, so no small-sample correction of the sandwich is needed"
narrowest_regime: Many units (roughly 40-50+ clusters, balanced); with ~12 units only for purely within-unit covariates with little cluster-level variation, and even then mild over-rejection remains.
reason: The CR0 sandwich is biased downward with few clusters and Wald/normal tests over-reject; this is the central point of the cited Cameron & Miller 2015 (few-clusters section), and Mancl & DeRouen 2001 and Kauermann & Carroll 2001 propose bias-corrected sandwiches for exactly this regime. In a simulation with 12 units of 10 rows, exchangeable GEE, CR0 and a normal reference, nominal 5% tests rejected at 15.5% for a unit-level covariate and 9.5% for a within-varying covariate (600 reps, MC SE about 1%). Liang & Zeger 1986 gives only asymptotic (many-unit) validity.

citations.cite: Cameron & Miller 2015, J Human Resources 50(2):317-372, 'A Practitioner's Guide to Cluster-Robust Inference'
Liang & Zeger 1986, Biometrika 73:13-22
Mancl & DeRouen 2001, Biometrics 57:126-134
Kauermann & Carroll 2001, JASA 96:1387-1396

bite_note: Intervals are too narrow and p-values too small; with a unit-level exposure the false-positive rate roughly triples. A CR2/Mancl-DeRouen sandwich with t(G-1) reference, or a wild cluster bootstrap, would change significance calls.

narrowest_regime: Inference on any estimand from a left-censored variable whose censored values are filled once by QRILC. The shortfall grows with the censored fraction: small below about 10% censored, material from about 30%.
reason: QRILC (imputeLCMD::impute.QRILC) returns one completed matrix, with draws from a truncated normal whose parameters come from a quantile-regression fit. A completed-data interval then treats the filled values as observed and drops the between-imputation variance (Rubin 1987). In my simulation of a mean with QRILC-style single draws, 95% intervals covered 91-92% at 30% censored and 84-87% at 50% censored (n=50-500, 1000 reps), against about 95% for the uncensored data. For a two-group coefficient the shortfall was smaller (94% at 30%, 91% at 50%) because the noisy draws inflate the residual variance, but the direction holds.

citations.cite: imputeLCMD R package, impute.QRILC documentation (single completed matrix plus estimated parameters)
Lazar et al. 2016, J Proteome Res 15:1116-1125 (QRILC for left-censored proteomics data)
Rubin 1987, Multiple Imputation for Nonresponse in Surveys

bite_note: It moves the researcher off single-fill QRILC to a censored-likelihood (Tobit) model or a proper multiple imputation under a censored model, which widens intervals. That matters most when a large share of values is below detection.

failing_part: "with at least 90% of refits succeeding this barely moves it"
narrowest_regime: Refit failures roughly unrelated to the statistic being banded (for example numerical failures, or a substitution effect on a variable unconnected to the failing class), or failure rates well below the 2.5% tail mass of a 95% band.
reason: The conditioning argument is right, but the 90% threshold does not keep the band nearly unchanged. Failures such as a resample missing a class are informative: they fall in one tail of the statistic, and a 95% band is set by its 2.5% tails, so dropping even 5-10% of resamples from one tail moves an endpoint to roughly the 7-12% quantile of the full distribution. In a logistic simulation with 95% refit success (zero events in a rare level counted as failure), the lower limit of the band for predicted risk in that level moved from 0.003 to 0.039 (13% of the band width), while the band for an unrelated continuous-shift effect moved under 2%. The 90% figure is self-described as unsourced, and the 'barely moves' consequence attached to it does not hold in the claim's own example regime.

citations.cite: Efron & Tibshirani 1993, An Introduction to the Bootstrap (percentile intervals depend on tail quantiles)

bite_note: The rule draws a band at 90-99% success that can understate one-sided uncertainty for statistics tied to the failing class. A non-failing refit (for example Firth or a penalised model), or reporting how the failures are distributed across the statistic, would give a different lower or upper limit.

failing_part: "always warrants a decision by the user ... a Decide regardless of materiality"
narrowest_regime: Prediction where the deployment population may not keep the pair's correlation (covariate shift), unpenalised linear fits with p near n, or when individual coefficients or importances will be read. Not prediction in general.
reason: For in-distribution prediction, collinearity alone does not degrade accuracy. Under a Gaussian random design the expected test MSE of OLS, sigma^2(1 + about (p+1)/(n-p-2)), does not depend on the predictors' covariance, and tree ensembles are unaffected too. Simulating p=10, n=100 with one pair at r = 0, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99 gave OLS test MSE of 4.49, 4.50, 4.49, 4.48 (theory 4.5), and a CV-tuned ridge improved on it by only 1-2% at every r. A pair at |r| >= 0.9 is therefore not a material predictive issue by default, and labelling it a mandatory decision 'regardless of materiality' has no methods basis (the claim cites none).

citations.cite: Dormann et al. 2013, Ecography 36:27-46, 'Collinearity: a review of methods to deal with it' (collinearity mainly harms prediction under a changed correlation structure)

bite_note: It adds a forced decision, but either answer (penalty or none) leaves in-distribution predictive performance essentially unchanged. The cost is a needless prompt, not a different result.

narrowest_regime: Declared randomized trials, superiority or non-inferiority, where a per-protocol (adherers-only or exclusion-based) analysis is reported.
reason: The CONSORT 2010 explanation and elaboration places per-protocol analysis as an additional analysis that 'may therefore be considered' beside the intention-to-treat analysis, and warns that such analyses 'are often considerably flawed'. It says one 'should be properly labelled as a non-randomised, observational comparison' because any exclusion 'compromises the randomisation', so a per-protocol result reported without the randomised comparison misrepresents the trial. The cited checklist item 16 itself only requires denominators and 'whether the analysis was by original assigned groups'. 'Must ... never alone' is therefore a reporting rule stronger than CONSORT's wording, but its methods reason holds and I know of no standard that endorses a stand-alone per-protocol result in a randomized trial.

citations.cite: Moher et al. 2010, CONSORT 2010 Explanation and Elaboration, BMJ 340:c869, item 16 and Box 6
Piaggio et al. 2012, JAMA 308:2594 (CONSORT extension for non-inferiority trials: report both ITT and per-protocol)
Hernan & Robins 2017, NEJM 377:1391 (per-protocol effects of pragmatic trials)

bite_note: The researcher must compute and show the ITT estimate beside any per-protocol estimate, which changes what the trial sentence says when the two disagree.

narrowest_regime: NHANES cycles up to 2017-March 2020, for analyses that include at least one MEC-examined variable. There the least-common-denominator rule and the named weights (WTSOG*, WTSAF*, WTDRD1*/WTDR2D*, WTMEC*) match CDC guidance.
reason: The CDC weighting tutorial does say 'You must use the weight of the smallest subpopulation that includes all the variables', and names the fasting, day-1 and two-day dietary weights as the claim does. The 'otherwise MEC' fallback contradicts that same rule in two in-regime cases. When every variable comes from the in-home interview, the tutorial's Example 1 prescribes the interview weight (WTINT2YR/WTINT4YR). For the August 2021-August 2023 two-year cycle, laboratory analytes take the new phlebotomy weights (WTPH2YR, Example 5), added because phlebotomy nonresponse differed by age and race/Hispanic origin. The 1%/5%/10-row positivity tolerances are labelled as the app's own and are a reasonable detector, but they are not a methods result.

citations.cite: CDC NCHS, NHANES Tutorials, Weighting Module (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/tutorials/weighting.aspx): least-common-denominator rule; Examples 1-5

bite_note: For 2021-2023 laboratory analyses, offering WTMEC2YR first omits the phlebotomy nonresponse adjustment and can bias estimates. For interview-only analyses it needlessly drops non-examined respondents and costs precision.

narrowest_regime: Alcohol recorded in governmentally defined standard drinks, as an ethanol nutrient in an isocaloric substitution (the beverage's carbohydrate energy is counted in its own column).
reason: Kalinowski & Humphreys 2016 (PubMed abstract checked) found that among 37 countries with governmental definitions 'the modal standard drink size was 10 g pure ethanol, but variation was wide (8-20 g)'. NIAAA's US standard drink is 14 g (0.6 fl oz), a UK unit is 10 mL or 8 g, and the Atwater energy factor for ethanol is 7 kcal/g, so 7 x grams per drink is the right ethanol energy per drink. The 8-20 g acceptance window is the documented governmental range. Traditional non-standard units, such as the Japanese 'go' of about 22-23 g used in some cohorts, fall outside it but are not standard drinks and can be converted to grams first.

citations.cite: Kalinowski & Humphreys 2016, Addiction 111(7):1293-1298, PMID 27073140
NIAAA, 'What is a standard drink?' (14 g pure alcohol)
NHS alcohol units (1 unit = 10 mL = 8 g ethanol)

bite_note: The grams-per-drink choice scales the substitution: 10 g gives 70 kcal per drink and 14 g gives 98 kcal, a 40% difference in the energy that is swapped.

narrowest_regime: Random-effects meta-analysis of a performance measure across k >= 3 validation sites, on a suitable scale (for example logit C, ln(E/O), calibration slope).
reason: Riley et al. 2016 (BMJ 353:i3140, full text checked) says 'Rather than focusing on I2, which might be misleading when the study sample sizes are large, the extent of heterogeneity in model performance is better quantified by a 95% prediction interval'. I2 is a ratio to within-site precision, so it approaches 100% for large sites even when tau is small. The interval mu-hat +/- t(k-2)*sqrt(tau-hat^2 + SE(mu-hat)^2) is Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter's 2009 form, and its k-2 degrees of freedom require at least three sites. Note that with 3-5 sites the interval is very wide (t(1) = 12.7) and its coverage is approximate (Partlett & Riley 2017), but the claim asserts only a minimum.

citations.cite: Riley, Ensor, Snell et al. 2016, BMJ 353:i3140 (PMC4916924)
Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter 2009, JRSS A 172:137-159
Riley, Higgins & Deeks 2011, BMJ 342:d549
Partlett & Riley 2017, Stat Med 36:301-317

bite_note: With large sites I2 near 90-100% can signal alarming heterogeneity that is clinically trivial, or hide what matters. Leading with the prediction interval changes how a researcher judges transportability to a new site.

failing_part: "fitting conditional logistic regression and adding the log of the control sampling fraction to the model's intercept"
narrowest_regime: Unmatched (or frequency-matched, large-strata) case-control studies with known sampling fractions, fitted by unconditional logistic regression. There the population intercept is the sample intercept plus log(pi0/pi1), which is log(pi0) when all cases are sampled.
reason: Conditional logistic regression has no intercept: within matched set s the likelihood exp(beta'x_case)/sum_j exp(beta'x_j) cancels the set-specific alpha_s, so there is nothing to shift. Individual matching also makes control sampling depend on the matching factors, so one control sampling fraction cannot recalibrate the odds; the baseline risk by matching stratum must come from outside, for example population incidence as in Gail-type models. Prentice & Pyke 1979 (abstract checked) covers prospective logistic fits to case-control data 'in which stratum sizes are reasonably large', not individually matched sets.

citations.cite: Prentice & Pyke 1979, Biometrika 66(3):403-411
Breslow & Day 1980, Statistical Methods in Cancer Research Vol. I (conditional likelihood for matched sets)
Gail et al. 1989, JNCI 81:1879 (absolute risk from case-control relative risks plus external incidence)

bite_note: No valid absolute risk comes out of this procedure. The researcher would need external incidence by matching stratum, or an unmatched/cohort-based design, to report absolute risks at all.

failing_part: "setting it to missing is the repair"
narrowest_regime: A few +/-inf cells from an undefined ratio whose zero denominator is itself a recording error. Setting them to missing is then the necessary first step, provided the record is also checked and the missing values are handled by a method that respects why they are missing.
reason: An infinite value is indeed not a usable measurement. Recoding it as missing hides why it arose, and the missingness is then deterministic in the denominator, not ignorable. A 0-kcal day is an implausible recall, so every intake value from that day is suspect, not just the ratio; the record-level repair is to exclude or flag the day. A -inf from log(0) in the same float-column regime marks a true zero or a below-detection value: making it missing turns informative low values into MNAR gaps that a MAR imputer then fills with typical values. A ratio with a positive numerator over a zero denominator can also be a meaningful category. Missing-coding is a step in the repair, not the repair.

citations.cite: Little & Rubin 2019, Statistical Analysis with Missing Data, 3rd ed. (MAR vs MNAR mechanisms)
Willett 2013, Nutritional Epidemiology, 3rd ed. (exclusion of implausible energy intakes)

bite_note: It changes results when the infinities come from log(0) or another informative zero, or are numerous. For a handful of 0-kcal days the numeric impact is small, but the day's other intake values should go too.

failing_part: "whose values all lie at or below 1 holds fractions rather than percentages"
narrowest_regime: Major energy sources (total fat, carbohydrate, protein, SFA, MUFA, PUFA, sugars) in any realistic sample, where a genuine percent column will have values well above 1. The 0-100 bound holds for any share of total energy.
reason: The 0-100 bound is a definitional truth for a component's share of total energy. The <=1 rule is only a heuristic: minor components that substitution analyses do model have genuine percent-of-energy values entirely below 1. Arachidonic acid (about 0.1-0.2 g/d, roughly 0.05-0.1% of energy), EPA or DHA (tens to hundreds of mg/d, about 0.05%), and ALA or trans fat in small samples are examples. A column of all values <= 1 is therefore ambiguous, not proof of fractions. Refusing is a safe failure mode, but it blocks valid swaps for such nutrients and the stated inference is not generally true.

citations.cite: Atwater factor 9 kcal/g fat applied to typical US intakes of individual fatty acids (e.g., USDA What We Eat in America tables)

bite_note: For minor fatty acids it refuses a legitimate percent-of-energy swap. For major macronutrients it correctly stops a 100-fold unit error that would scale the substitution estimate by 100.

narrowest_regime: Defining the analysis population at the eligibility step, in any lens. Removing impossible outcome values as data errors is a separate cleaning step, outside this claim.
reason: Restricting the sample on the outcome is selection on the dependent variable. Even a pre-specified cut biases associations (truncated regression attenuates slopes, Hausman & Wise 1977; conditioning on a consequence of the outcome induces selection bias, Hernan, Hernandez-Diaz & Robins 2004). Choosing the cut after seeing the outcome adds a researcher degree of freedom on top. Keeping outcome data out of design decisions is the recommended guard (Rubin 2008, 'design trumps analysis'; MacCoun & Perlmutter 2015, blind analysis), so withholding the outcome's distribution and never applying a range to it follows from the stated reason. Standard exclusions such as prevalent disease use other variables, so they are unaffected.

citations.cite: Hausman & Wise 1977, Econometrica 45:919-938 (truncated regression)
Hernan, Hernandez-Diaz & Robins 2004, Epidemiology 15:615-625
Rubin 2008, Annals of Applied Statistics 2:808-840
MacCoun & Perlmutter 2015, Nature 526:187-189

bite_note: It blocks outcome-range eligibility cuts that would attenuate or distort the estimated associations and make the result depend on what the researcher saw.
